hints: Look carefully at where X is. It is on one single strand, joining one nucleotide down to the next, between a pentagon (sugar) and a small circle.
Remember what makes the sugar-phosphate backbone: a phosphate group forms two ester links, one to each neighbouring sugar.
walkthrough:
**Read the diagram like a map**

Look at the three parts of a nucleotide. The pentagon is deoxyribose sugar, the small circle is phosphate, the rectangle is the base.

X is bracketing the link that joins one whole nucleotide to the next one down in the same strand.

**Recall the backbone bond**

The backbone of DNA is a repeating sugar-phosphate chain. Adjacent nucleotides are joined by a strong covalent bond from the sugar of one to the phosphate of the next.

Because the phosphate is linked by two ester bonds, one to each sugar, we call it a phosphodiester bond.

**Pick the answer**

X is that backbone link between nucleotides in one strand, so it must be phosphodiester. That is option D.

options.A: Glycosidic bond joins the base (rectangle) to its own sugar (pentagon), not one nucleotide to the next.
options.B: Hydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together between bases, they are not found along a single strand backbone like X.
options.C: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, they are never found in DNA.
options.D: Correct. X links the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone. This is the phosphodiester bond.
